_meta.purpose: Cited research provenance for the clerkship-agent vitals-escalation pack. Sourced via the GATE-A spec Appendix A prompt (run by the CSO in a web-enabled session, 2026-06-17). The runtime pack docs/clinical/agent/vitals-escalation.json is DISTILLED from this (engine shape + catalog-mapped escalation features). NOT clinical content authored from model memory — every threshold is cited here; needs_cso_input entries await CSO ratification before AGENT_VITALS_ESCALATION_CSO_SIGNED is set.

alt.note: ESC 2024 uses >=180/110; AHA/ACC lineage uses >=180/120 — see needs_cso_input

baseTier.label: Severe hypertension / markedly elevated BP (no organ-damage features)
baseTier.action: Confirm with repeat reading after rest; do NOT lower acutely/aggressively if asymptomatic (risk of harm); arrange/optimise oral therapy and timely outpatient follow-up; screen for target-organ damage.

anyOf: severe headache, visual disturbance, confusion or seizures (encephalopathy)
reduced urine output / acute kidney injury

tier.label: Hypertensive EMERGENCY (acute hypertension-mediated target-organ damage)
ddx: acute coronary syndrome / acute LV failure / pulmonary oedema
tier.action: EMERGENCY: controlled IV BP reduction (agent + target by the specific syndrome — e.g. NOT aggressive lowering in acute ischaemic stroke; rapid control in dissection/eclampsia/pulmonary oedema); urgent investigations (ECG, U&E/creatinine, urinalysis, fundoscopy, imaging as indicated); admit (ICU/HDU). Decisions are syndrome-specific — clinician-led.

entries.ugandaNote: Eclampsia is a leading obstetric emergency — any pregnant/recently-postpartum woman with high BP + features needs MgSO4 + BP control + delivery planning per Uganda Clinical Guidelines (use MEOWS, not NEWS2, in pregnancy). CT/MRI to distinguish stroke type is often unavailable — treat the syndrome clinically and refer; IV antihypertensive choice depends on locally-available agents. RHD/CKD common as background.

citation.guideline: ESC Guidelines for the management of elevated blood pressure and hypertension; AHA Scientific Statement on management of elevated BP in the acute care setting; 2017 ACC/AHA Hypertension Guideline

entries.cso_reason: Guidelines disagree on the diastolic emergency cut-point: ESC 2024 defines emergency at >=180/110 mmHg; AHA/ACC lineage uses >=180/120 mmHg. Both provided; CSO to set MedSync's flag threshold and confirm alignment with the Uganda Clinical Guidelines.

tiers.note: NEWS2 single-parameter red score 3; common shock threshold

baseTier.label: Hypotension (isolated low systolic BP)
baseTier.action: Confirm reading + posture; assess perfusion (pulse, capillary refill, mentation, urine output); look for a cause; fluid as indicated by volume status. Reassess — trend matters more than a single value.

anyOf: tachycardia + cool peripheries / prolonged capillary refill / mottling
raised JVP + muffled heart sounds (tamponade) / unilateral absent breath sounds (tension pneumothorax)

tier.label: SHOCK / haemodynamic compromise
ddx: hypovolaemic shock (haemorrhage, GI loss, severe dehydration)
obstructive shock (tension pneumothorax, tamponade, massive PE)
tier.action: EMERGENCY: ABCDE, high-flow oxygen, large-bore IV access, restore circulation per cause; if sepsis suspected — cultures + early antibiotics + measured resuscitation; treat the specific shock type (e.g. adrenaline for anaphylaxis, decompression for tension pneumothorax, control haemorrhage); senior help; admit ICU/HDU.

entries.ugandaNote: Severe malaria, severe anaemia (incl. sickle cell crisis), GI bleeding, and obstetric haemorrhage are major shock causes. CRITICAL: in febrile children with impaired perfusion, the FEAST trial showed rapid fluid boluses INCREASED mortality — do NOT bolus febrile non-hypotensive children; follow WHO/Uganda paediatric guidance. Lactate and blood products may be unavailable — clinical perfusion assessment is primary.

citation.guideline: Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3) / qSOFA; Surviving Sepsis Campaign; Royal College of Physicians NEWS2; WHO/FEAST (paediatric fluids)
citation.version: Sepsis-3 2016; SSC current; RCP NEWS2 2017; FEAST 2011

entries.cso_reason: Two cut-points in use (<=100 mmHg for the sepsis/qSOFA screen vs <=90 mmHg as the NEWS2 red/shock threshold). CSO to set MedSync's flag band and confirm the paediatric FEAST guardrail is encoded for febrile children.

trigger.scale2_note: For patients with a target of 88-92% (e.g. COPD/hypercapnic risk), use NEWS2 SpO2 Scale 2 — different bands; CSO/clinician to select the scale.

baseTier.label: Hypoxaemia (low oxygen saturation)
ddx: anaemia (may read normal SpO2 despite low O2 content)
baseTier.action: Confirm with a good trace; give controlled oxygen to a target (88-92% if hypercapnic risk, else 94-98%); identify + treat the cause; reassess RR and work of breathing together (SpO2 alone underestimates respiratory distress).

anyOf: unable to speak full sentences / exhaustion / silent chest
altered mental status / agitation or drowsiness (CO2 retention)

tier.label: Acute respiratory failure / impending arrest
tier.action: EMERGENCY: ABCDE, high-flow/titrated oxygen, treat the cause urgently (e.g. bronchodilators, decompress tension pneumothorax); consider ventilatory support (NIV/intubation); senior + critical-care help; admit.

entries.ugandaNote: TB, HIV-associated pneumonia (incl. PCP) and severe malaria are key causes. Altitude (parts of Uganda are elevated) lowers baseline SpO2 — interpret against local normals. Pulse oximeters, oxygen supply and ventilatory support may be limited — prioritise oxygen and referral; in severe anaemia, SpO2 can be normal despite inadequate oxygen delivery.

citation.guideline: Royal College of Physicians National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2); BTS Guideline for oxygen use in adults

entries.cso_reason: Scale 1 vs Scale 2 selection is patient-dependent (hypercapnic/COPD risk) and altitude shifts baseline normals — CSO to define how MedSync selects the scale and whether to apply an altitude/locale adjustment.

baseTier.label: Abnormal respiratory rate (tachypnoea or bradypnoea)
baseTier.action: RR is the most sensitive early deterioration sign — count for a full minute. Identify the cause; treat (oxygen, bronchodilators, reverse opioids if indicated); reassess with SpO2 and work of breathing. A rising RR is an early warning even when other vitals are normal.

anyOf: RR <=8 with reduced consciousness (impending arrest / opioid toxicity)

tier.label: Respiratory failure / peri-arrest
tier.action: EMERGENCY: ABCDE; oxygen; treat the cause (bronchodilators, naloxone for opioid toxicity, fluids+insulin for DKA per protocol); ventilatory support if needed; senior/critical-care help; admit.

entries.ugandaNote: Kussmaul breathing in a young person points to DKA (often new-onset, late-presenting) or salicylate/toxin; severe malaria and pneumonia cause respiratory distress; acidotic 'respiratory distress' in malaria is a danger sign. Respiratory support is often limited — early recognition and referral are key.

citation.guideline: Royal College of Physicians National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2)

baseTier.label: Bradycardia
ddx: raised intracranial pressure (with hypertension = Cushing response)
baseTier.action: 12-lead ECG; review medications + electrolytes; assess for symptoms/perfusion. Asymptomatic with good perfusion — investigate cause. Treat reversible causes.

tier.label: Adverse/unstable bradycardia
ddx: complete (3rd-degree) or Mobitz II AV block
tier.action: EMERGENCY per resuscitation-council adult bradycardia algorithm: assess for adverse features; atropine; if refractory, transcutaneous pacing / chronotropic infusion; treat toxic/electrolyte cause; senior + cardiology; continuous monitoring.

entries.ugandaNote: Consider hyperkalaemia (AKI, severe illness) and drug toxicity; pacing facilities are often unavailable — stabilise medically (atropine, treat hyperkalaemia) and refer urgently. Hypothermia from severe illness/neonatal context can cause bradycardia.

citation.guideline: Royal College of Physicians NEWS2; Resuscitation Council adult bradycardia algorithm

baseTier.label: Tachycardia
baseTier.action: 12-lead ECG to define rhythm; identify + treat the cause (it is often a compensatory sign — find what it is compensating for); reassess BP and perfusion. Treat the cause, not just the number.

anyOf: rate >150 with a broad or irregular complex (unstable tachyarrhythmia)

tier.label: Unstable tachyarrhythmia / decompensation
ddx: septic or hypovolaemic shock with compensatory tachycardia
tier.action: EMERGENCY: ABCDE; if a tachyarrhythmia with adverse features — synchronised DC cardioversion per the resuscitation-council algorithm; if compensatory — treat the underlying shock/sepsis/haemorrhage; senior help; monitoring; admit.

entries.ugandaNote: Sepsis (malaria, pneumonia, typhoid), severe anaemia and dehydration are very common drivers — treat the cause. Rheumatic heart disease and thyrotoxicosis cause AF. Distinguish a compensatory sinus tachycardia (don't 'rate-control') from a primary arrhythmia.

citation.guideline: Royal College of Physicians NEWS2; Resuscitation Council adult tachycardia algorithm

baseTier.label: Fever / pyrexia
baseTier.action: Identify the source (history, exam, focused tests); in an endemic area, TEST FOR MALARIA (RDT/film) in any fever; antipyretics for comfort; reassess for sepsis features. Fever alone is a symptom — the priority is finding and treating the cause.

tier.label: SEPSIS / serious infection (e.g. meningitis, severe malaria)
tier.action: EMERGENCY: treat as sepsis — cultures + EARLY broad-spectrum antibiotics, measured fluid resuscitation, oxygen, source control; if meningitis suspected don't delay antibiotics; if malaria — IV artesunate; senior help; admit. Use a sepsis screen (e.g. qSOFA/NEWS2) but treat on clinical suspicion.

entries.ugandaNote: Malaria must be actively excluded in EVERY fever (RDT/microscopy) — and severe/cerebral malaria treated with IV artesunate per WHO/Uganda guidance. Typhoid, TB, HIV-related infections and meningitis (incl. cryptococcal in HIV) are common. FEAST: do NOT give rapid fluid boluses to febrile non-hypotensive children. Antibiotic + artesunate availability and blood cultures vary by facility.

citation.guideline: Surviving Sepsis Campaign; Sepsis-3/qSOFA; WHO Guidelines for malaria; Uganda Clinical Guidelines
citation.version: SSC current; Sepsis-3 2016; WHO malaria 2025; UCG current

baseTier.label: Low temperature / hypothermia (<=35.0 C)
ddx: sepsis (hypothermia is a sepsis sign, especially in the elderly/immunocompromised)
baseTier.action: Confirm with a low-reading thermometer (core); rewarm; CRUCIALLY look for an underlying cause — hypothermia in an unwell adult often signals sepsis, not just cold. Check glucose. Reassess.

tier.label: Hypothermic sepsis / myxoedema coma / decompensation
tier.action: EMERGENCY: ABCDE; active rewarming; treat sepsis (cultures + early antibiotics + resuscitation) if infection suspected; correct glucose; if myxoedema coma — thyroid hormone + steroids per protocol; cardiac monitoring (arrhythmia risk); senior help; admit.

entries.ugandaNote: Hypothermia as a sign of severe sepsis/severe illness (and in neonates) is important; myxoedema is rarer but missed. Core thermometers and warming may be limited — improvise warming and prioritise treating sepsis/glucose. Always check capillary glucose.

citation.guideline: Royal College of Physicians NEWS2; Surviving Sepsis Campaign

tiers.label: Level 3
tiers.note: any glucose with altered mental/physical function requiring assistance - clinical, not a number

baseTier.label: Hypoglycaemia (Level 1: 3.0-3.8 mmol/L)
baseTier.action: Treat immediately with fast-acting oral carbohydrate (15-20 g) if conscious and able to swallow; recheck in ~15 min and repeat until >=4.0 mmol/L; then a longer-acting carbohydrate; find and address the cause (review insulin/sulfonylurea). Always check glucose in any unwell or altered patient ('Don't Ever Forget Glucose').

anyOf: unable to swallow / reduced consciousness / coma
requires assistance from another person (Level 3 / severe)

tier.label: Severe hypoglycaemia (Level 2/3) - neuroglycopenic emergency
tier.action: EMERGENCY: if IV access - IV glucose (e.g. dextrose) per protocol; if no IV access - IM glucagon; recheck and repeat; protect airway; in sulfonylurea/recurrent cases admit and consider octreotide; treat the cause. Recheck glucose after recovery - relapse is common.

entries.ugandaNote: Hypoglycaemia is a key danger sign in severe malaria (and quinine therapy) and in sick neonates/children - check glucose in every unwell patient. Sulfonylureas (e.g. glibenclamide) cause prolonged, recurrent hypoglycaemia - admit. IV dextrose / IM glucagon availability varies; oral sugar is the universal first step if able to swallow.

citation.guideline: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care - Glycemic Goals and Hypoglycemia / Diabetes Care in the Hospital

entries.cso_reason: Glucose thresholds are point-of-care-meter and unit dependent (mmol/L vs mg/dL; capillary vs venous bias). CSO to confirm the assay/units used in MedSync facilities and the exact treatment doses (which live in the prescribing engine, not here).

alt_unit.note: >10.0 mmol/L (>180 mg/dL) is 'time above range'; a flag band ~>11 mmol/L is commonly used - CSO to set

marked.note: marked hyperglycaemia; check ketones - context for DKA/HHS

baseTier.label: Hyperglycaemia
baseTier.action: Confirm; CHECK KETONES (blood beta-hydroxybutyrate ideally, or urine) and hydration; assess for an intercurrent illness/infection; review/adjust therapy; arrange follow-up. Marked or symptomatic hyperglycaemia + ketones needs the DKA/HHS pathway.

anyOf: very high glucose with marked dehydration (HHS, often >30 mmol/L)

tier.label: Hyperglycaemic EMERGENCY (DKA or HHS)
tier.action: EMERGENCY: confirm with ketones/venous gas/U&E; manage per the current DKA/HHS consensus pathway - IV fluids, fixed-rate IV insulin (or SC for mild/uncomplicated DKA where appropriate), potassium replacement, treat the precipitant, monitor closely; senior help; admit (HDU/ICU as needed). Doses/rates via protocol + the prescribing engine.

entries.ugandaNote: New-onset diabetes often presents LATE as DKA; check ketones in any marked hyperglycaemia. Blood ketone meters and venous-gas analysers may be unavailable - use urine ketones + clinical judgement and refer. Treat any precipitating infection (incl. malaria). Doses are guideline-version sensitive (2024 DKA/HHS consensus changed criteria + allows SC insulin for mild DKA) - verify at build.

citation.guideline: ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS Consensus on Hyperglycemic Crises (DKA/HHS); ADA Standards of Care; WHO/Uganda Clinical Guidelines
citation.version: Hyperglycaemic crises consensus 2024; ADA 2024-2026; UCG current

entries.cso_reason: The hyperglycaemia FLAG band (e.g. >11 vs >14 mmol/L) is not a single fixed guideline value and is assay/unit dependent; the DKA/HHS diagnostic thresholds + treatment doses are guideline-version sensitive and live in the prescribing engine. CSO to set the flag band and confirm the pathway/criteria at build.

trigger.avpu_equivalent: any level below Alert on AVPU/ACVPU (i.e. new Confusion, Voice, Pain, Unresponsive) = NEWS2 score 3 (red)

tiers.note: any drop below 15 / new confusion - abnormal, flag
AIRWAY AT RISK - cannot protect airway; emergency

baseTier.label: Reduced conscious level / new confusion (GCS <=14 or below Alert)
baseTier.action: ABCDE; CHECK GLUCOSE IMMEDIATELY ('Don't Ever Forget Glucose'); check SpO2; review medications/toxins; focused neuro exam; identify and treat reversible causes; serial GCS (a trend matters). Note: scoring 0 on NEWS2 does NOT mean normal - assess clinically.

anyOf: signs of raised ICP (Cushing response: hypertension + bradycardia)

tier.label: Critical: airway-threatening / acute brain emergency
ddx: acute stroke / intracranial haemorrhage / raised ICP
tier.action: EMERGENCY: ABCDE with AIRWAY PROTECTION (GCS <=8 - secure the airway / call for anaesthetic-airway help); correct glucose + oxygen immediately; treat the cause (e.g. naloxone, anticonvulsant, antibiotics +/- antimalarial for CNS infection); urgent imaging if available; senior + critical-care help; admit.

entries.ugandaNote: Cerebral malaria, meningitis (bacterial + cryptococcal in HIV), hypoglycaemia and stroke are leading causes - and hypoglycaemia + cerebral malaria are reversible/treatable, so check glucose and a malaria test in EVERY reduced-consciousness patient. CT is frequently unavailable to distinguish stroke type - treat clinically and refer. The 'GCS <=8 - protect airway' rule holds even where intubation is limited (positioning, airway adjuncts, urgent referral).

citation.guideline: Royal College of Physicians NEWS2 (ACVPU); Glasgow Coma Scale; WHO/Uganda Clinical Guidelines (cerebral malaria, meningitis)
citation.version: RCP NEWS2 2017; GCS (Teasdale); WHO malaria 2025; UCG current
